lede: This parser reads JSON that has not finished arriving. Bytes come in whatever pieces a socket or a model hands over, and the value built from them has to be readable *between* pieces rather than at the end. That rules out the usual shape — read the document, then walk it — which is what `Decodable` assumes, and it rules out a SAX parser too, since those emit a value only once it is complete.

So the parser is a state machine fed chunks. Every call consumes exactly the bytes it was given, emits every token those bytes finish, and leaves enough behind to resume in the middle of one: a number split across two chunks, a `\u00e9` split down the middle. Almost everything below is about keeping that contract without paying for it.

how.title: A chunk arrives, and the parser picks up mid-token
how.detail: `parse(_:into:)` takes a pointer and a count, and returns when those bytes are gone rather than when the document ends. A chunk that stops inside a token leaves the state machine there; a UTF-8 sequence cut in half is held in one 64-bit field and completed against the next chunk's first bytes. `finish(into:)` is the other end, where a trailing number completes and an unclosed string or container is reported.

how.title: A switch over thirteen states, and structural bytes taken in runs
detail: `parse` is 1284 bytes, 322 instructions, 18 calls and no vector instruction: it decides what the next byte is and calls the function for that token class. A byte's cost is that round trip rather than its own work — so `},{"` and `":`, a fifth of token dense JSON and always in clusters, are taken by a loop that stays put while the state is structural, and a value that finishes inside the chunk is settled there too.

For the length of a run the state, the depth and the container stack sit in locals, the stack being one `UInt64` whose bit *n* says whether depth *n* is an object — which is why nesting stops at sixty-four rather than spilling. Where the input is dense one NEON classification of sixty-four bytes replaces the scans in front of each token. A fully windowed walk exists behind a threshold and is off by default: it loses 4–36% wherever a document is not structurally dense.

how.title: Whitespace and string content are scanned sixteen bytes at a time
detail: Every whitespace byte is ≤ 0x20 and every byte that may legally follow one is > 0x20, so minified input settles the question with one inline compare and never touches a vector; only what survives goes out of line to the SIMD16 scan. None of `canada` is whitespace and 71% of `citm_catalog` is — how much there is to find is a property of the document, not of JSON.

Strings take the same shape: one pass over sixteen bytes tests the closing quote, a backslash and a control byte together, and a movemask names the lane that hit. A `\n` is decoded inline and a `\uXXXX` through a call — five bytes of work can afford one and one byte cannot, and spelling both inline cost an escape heavy payload 18.5%. Non-ASCII leaves with the end index, for a vector UTF-8 validator built out of three table lookups.

how.title: A number is scanned greedily, then parsed by the narrowest kernel that fits it
how.detail: One pass finds the token's end. An unsigned integer of up to eight digits is parsed with no loop and no data dependent branch, from the eight bytes *ending* at the token: those are already consumed input, so one `end >= 8` test makes the read safe and the bytes masked off become leading zeros. Floats are accumulated and finished by Eisel-Lemire rather than a `String` round trip. Either way the number is emitted once and whole — `1`, `12`, `123` are not prefixes of the value the way partial string content is.

how.title: Finished tokens cross one boundary, and the destination may decline
how.detail: A sink gets one call per token carrying a borrowed `Span<UInt8>`, and those calls do not throw: a rejection is recorded and read once per chunk. Opening a container returns a disposition, so a sink with no use for a subtree answers `.skip` and the parser scans past it at structural speed — brackets matched by kind, no keys resolved, no values built. The close always arrives even then, so a sink is never left holding an unbalanced frame.

how.title: A key becomes a field by comparing words, into storage that can be read mid-parse
detail: Keys arrive whole and are matched against precomputed 64-bit words, one or two compares for most real keys, where `Dictionary` measured 7–8× slower because `Hasher` runs at every lookup. The read happens in place out of the parser's buffer, using padding it already had, and what the macro emits per member is data rather than a closure — so most fields are stored straight at `storage + offset`.

Frames hold pointers into the value being built, so every depth updates per byte. String bytes accumulate in blocks whose size doubles, and producing a `String` is a read. Reading a field while parsing continues is a borrowed view the compiler will not let outlive the call that lent it, so a leaf can be read without materializing the levels above it.

why.title: The first profile said the opposite of what was true
detail: The library started at 2.5–3.5 MB/s and every suspect was innocent. Key path dispatch was single digit percent. A naive byte-at-a-time switch already ran at 1520 MB/s, five times the target. A per-byte function call cost 0.28 ns, and copying a `Partial` per byte cost about 1%.

The cost was allocation and code that could not specialize: one malloc per byte of string content, roughly two more per byte from an unspecialized generic `Sequence` walk, and a read-modify-write of a whole subtree per byte through a computed key path. That is why the interface below is spans and stored properties rather than values and key paths — and it is where the habit of measuring everything in this log comes from, because the intuitions were not close.

why.title: The parse loop is register bound, not work bound
detail: Whitespace is found by looking ahead, one compare before every structural byte — which buys nothing on a minified document. Discovering it in the dispatch switch instead is free by construction: no lookahead, no flag, and a document with no whitespace pays literally zero. It was built, and it lost 10–18% nearly everywhere.

The lookahead has one whitespace test; discovery has five, one in each state that has to reject a byte it does not recognise, and that function inlines into the loop. `canada` has no whitespace at all, saved exactly what was predicted, and still lost 2%. One compare in one place beats zero compares in five places, and *where* code sits decides more of this parser's shape than how much work it does.

why.title: Runs, not bytes — and no structural bitmap
detail: SIMD16 beat a scalar loop at every run length measured, from 4 bytes (2476 against 1401 MB/s) to 4096 (21411 against 1548). SWAR loses to a scalar loop below about twelve bytes and never beats SIMD16, so it is unused on this path; SIMD32 loses because a NEON register is 128 bits and it lowers to two operations and a recombine.

Building a bitmap of every structural byte first, the way simdjson does, measured worse than testing bytes as they arrive: 2824 MB/s against 3788. Structural bytes are 20–25% of token dense JSON, so the bitmap is dense, and walking its set bits costs more than the tests it removes. The technique is sound; the density it assumes is not there.

why.title: A fusion only pays if it deletes a call
detail: Because a byte's cost is the round trip into the dispatcher, the wins are in not making the trip. Staying in a loop while the state remains structural took the corpus from 1071 to 1181 MB/s, and `canada` — nothing but `[`, `,` and numbers — gained 15% from a change that scans nothing.

The colon after a key looked like the next one: across 61,145 keys in the corpus not one has a space before its colon, so peeking for it hits 100% of the time. It moved the aggregate by 1 MB/s. The run loop had already swallowed the colon, and the value's opening quote still forced the call the fusion was supposed to delete. The comma passes that test — after it, the whitespace and the next value's first byte, nothing structural is left — and it is worth +4.7%.

why.title: Nothing about the destination's types reaches the parser
detail: The sink takes one token at a time as a borrowed span, and its methods do not throw: a failure is recorded and read once per chunk, because a check after every call sits on the hottest path in the program and measured 2–5%. Escapes are decoded to UTF-8 before they cross, so nothing below the boundary needs `String` or the Unicode tables — which is what lets the core build for Embedded Swift.

The boundary is also format agnostic: what crosses it are tokens, not JSON, so another parser can drive the same sinks. And because the destination is what answers, a sink can say it does not want a subtree at all and the parser will skip it at structural speed — worth +41% where most of what arrives is not being kept.

why.title: A partial that can be read decides how storage may move
detail: Frames hold pointers into the value being built, which is what lets a partial update per byte at every depth. It is sound only because the innermost open container is the only thing ever mutated: a buffer can move on its next append, and that cannot happen while an element of it is open. `Dictionary` breaks the rule outright, since an insertion can relocate every value, so the streaming dictionary is an append-only array that keeps insertion order and builds an index only past a threshold. Sharing is the same question from the writer's side, and it was answered wrongly once: a snapshot is a plain copy of the value, so every copy is also a writer, and an append that skipped its uniqueness check let two of them claim one slot. Restoring the check cost 9–13% on the rows that keep nothing.

Reading is the same constraint from the other side. A value handed out mid-parse shares the buffers still being written into, so keeping one means copying it: reading a member per byte through `current` costs 24 ms where parsing the same payload and observing nothing costs 449 µs. A borrowed view projects instead, copying per member actually read, at 459 µs — and it is `~Copyable`, so what stops it outliving the parser's storage is the compiler rather than a comment.

why.title: The experiments that lost are kept too
detail: Thirty of the recorded experiments were rejected against twenty-five landed, and several of the rejections are the counterintuitive ones above: a change that is free by construction, a fusion that hits 100% of the time, a word compare replacing a byte loop. Each is kept with the measurement that settled it, because the argument for building it is just as convincing the second time somebody makes it. The Experiments view above lists them together.

nodes.title: parse(_:into:)
why: Input arrives in pieces. An LLM streams a few bytes at a time and a socket hands over whatever has arrived, and a partial value has to be readable after every piece. So the parser cannot wait for the whole document and then walk it. Each call consumes the bytes it was given, emits everything those bytes finish, and leaves the parser in a state the next call can resume from.

This is where that contract is kept. Everything downstream works on one chunk, a base pointer and a count. `parse(_:into:)` decides how that chunk is walked, and makes sure the sink ends the call holding everything the chunk produced, including when the call throws.
prose: There are three entry points. The buffer form does one length test to pick a walk, then wraps the loop in a handler that settles a pending `stringBegin` and commits the sink before an error propagates. `parse(byte:)` first tests for byte-fed input's most common shape, an ordinary ASCII byte inside a string value, and emits it as one `stringChunk` without entering the dispatcher. `finish(into:)` is the other end: a document that ends in a number only finds out the number is complete there, and an unclosed string or container is reported there.

The ordering in the error handler matters. Everything emitted ahead of a grammar error still belongs to the sink, so a destination that rejected something earlier gets to report *its* failure rather than having the parser's take precedence.

The chunk's address is never stored. It is threaded down into the walk and on into every emission, because the run loop already holds it in a register. What the parser *does* store is laid out to a cache line, with everything a parse reads or writes in the first sixty-four bytes.

next.label: n ≥ windowThreshold
next.when: The chunk is large enough to index ahead of the walk. `parsePastThreshold` takes it, and runs `parseWindowed` unless a given-up block walk is due a re-probe, in which case it counts the chunk and walks it with the ordinary dispatcher.

next.label: otherwise
next.when: The ordinary path: the bytes are walked directly by `parseDispatching`, which is force-inlined so the loop's layout is what it was when it lived here.

next.label: on the way out
next.when: Both walks end the same way — `settlePendingStringBegin`, then `commitSink`, then the consumed-byte count advances. This also runs on the error path, which is the point: what was emitted before a grammar error still belongs to the sink.

nodes.invokes: One length test picks the walk, and the whole call is wrapped in a handler that commits to the sink before any error propagates.

steps.title: A call arrives
steps.detail: Two entry points share one state machine: `parse(_:into:)` takes a buffer and `parse(byte:into:)` takes a single byte. Neither reads anything before recording where the bytes are.

next.label: one byte, inside a string
next.when: The shape byte-fed input is mostly made of: an ordinary ASCII byte in a string value. Six tests deep — state, the byte's own range, then three parser fields — and it produces one record and one commit without the dispatcher or the scan.

next.label: a buffer
next.when: `parse(_:into:)`. An empty buffer returns having touched nothing.

steps.title: deliverStringByte
steps.detail: One `stringChunk` carrying the byte itself, written into the parser's reserved scratch, so there is no pointer to take. The byte's storage does not outlive the call, so `deliverStringByte` commits the sink before returning — which doubles as the call's failure check — and advances the consumed count itself. Anything that fails one of the six tests falls through to the per-byte `dispatchOnce` loop unchanged.

steps.title: the base is a parameter
steps.detail: The chunk's address is handed down into the walk and on into every emission rather than written to a field. `chunkBase` was that field, and it had exactly one reader — the function that builds a token's span — so reading it back there was a load from a cache line the run loop otherwise never touches, while the loop already held the pointer in a register. With the pointer arriving as an argument the span builder is `static`: nothing of the parser is left in the result, and keeping the old `@_lifetime(borrow self)` shape on a body that no longer reads `self` tripped a SIL ownership verifier crash in the `PartialSink` specialisation of the structural run.

steps.title: one cache line of state
steps.detail: Field order here is a cache-line decision, not a taste one. Everything a parse reads or writes lives in the first sixty-four bytes; past them sit `ownsBuffer`, which only the deinit reads, and the window telemetry, which is dead for any parser that never crosses `windowThreshold` — the default. The small fields are narrowed to their real ranges rather than bit-packed: narrowing is free on arm64, where `ldrb`/`ldrh` zero-extend, while packing per-byte state into shared words would turn plain stores into read-modify-writes on the string and unicode paths and break the store fusion the compiler already performs on the adjacent flags — it emits one `strh` for `isKeyToken` and `keyContainsNonASCII`. The buffer is split out of its `UnsafeMutableBufferPointer` so its capacity sits next to the count the append guard compares against: one eight-byte load answers both.

steps.title: n vs windowThreshold
steps.detail: One compare picks the walk. The threshold defaults to `Int.max`, so the windowed path is off unless a caller asks for it — with one exception: while a given-up structural block walk is waiting to be re-probed, the gate lowers the default to 4 KB so bulk-sized chunks are routed past it and counted.

next.label: n ≥ threshold
next.when: Long enough to be worth indexing 32 KB ahead of the walk, or a bulk chunk the lowered threshold sent to be counted.

next.label: n < threshold
next.when: The ordinary path: the dispatcher walks the bytes itself.

steps.title: parsePastThreshold
steps.detail: Out of line, so the test for a pending re-probe is not in front of every `parse` call. With a re-probe due it counts the chunk's kilobytes toward the 64 KB countdown and, if the gate lowered the threshold, walks the chunk with the dispatcher and commits exactly as `parse` does; otherwise it runs the indexed walk, whose own node covers what it does and why it is gated.

steps.title: parseDispatching
steps.detail: The switch-per-state loop that owns every token class.

steps.title: settle, then commit
steps.detail: A pending `stringBegin` is settled and `commit()` reaches the sink *before* a grammar error propagates. Everything emitted ahead of the error is still the sink's, so a destination that rejected something earlier reports its own failure rather than having the parser's take precedence.

next.label: the caller has no more bytes
next.when: `finish()` is a separate call, and the only one that can report a document that ended mid-token.

steps.title: finish()
steps.detail: The state the parser stopped in becomes the verdict: `.number` emits the buffered token, a string state is unterminated, `.literal` is invalid. The lifetime signal goes out before the structural checks, which deliver nothing new.

nodes.title: Chunk boundaries
why: A chunk boundary does not respect tokens. It can fall inside a string, halfway through a number, between the two halves of a `\uD83D\uDE00` surrogate pair, or inside a single multi-byte UTF-8 character. Every token class therefore has to be resumable, and the parser has to remember enough to finish what the previous chunk started.

Most of that memory is the `state` field, a few small counters (`literalIndex`, `unicodeRemaining`, `highSurrogate`) and the parser's buffer, which holds a key or a number the chunk cut. A cut UTF-8 character needs its own mechanism: spans handed to the sink end on a character boundary, so the leading bytes of a cut character can be neither emitted nor dropped.
prose: A chunk boundary can land anywhere, including inside a UTF-8 sequence. The parser holds the incomplete tail in a single 64-bit field — little-endian, a byte per lane — rather than guessing, and completes it against the next chunk's first bytes before the main loop starts.
This is the cost of streaming rather than batching, and it is kept to the edges: the resume path runs once per chunk, not once per byte, so the bulk loop never tests for it.

next.label: resume, then walk
next.when: `completePendingUTF8` finishes the held sequence against the new chunk's first bytes and returns the index the main loop starts from. With nothing held the loop starts at 0 and the test is one compare.

nodes.invokes: Runs once at the top of the next chunk's walk, before the loop starts — never per byte.

steps.title: trimmingIncompleteUTF8
steps.detail: Before a string run that reaches the end of the buffer is emitted, the last four bytes are walked backwards looking for a lead whose sequence the chunk cut. Nothing further back is examined, because no sequence is longer than four bytes. It is forced inline: byte-fed input ends every string run at the chunk end, so the string body asks this on every content byte, and left to the optimizer the serialized `consumeStringRun<PartialSink>` called it instead.

next.label: a lead is short of its bytes
next.when: The run's last bytes are the head of a sequence this chunk cut, so they are held back instead of emitted.

next.label: the run ends on a whole sequence
next.when: Nothing is pending and the run is emitted as it stands.

steps.title: emit the run
steps.detail: The common case, and the reason this test is where it is: it costs one backwards walk over at most four bytes per run, not per byte.

steps.title: holdPendingUTF8
steps.detail: At most four bytes packed little-endian into one field, a byte per lane, so completion appends at lane `have` with a shift rather than a store. It used to live in the last eight bytes of the parser's buffer — a full page away from everything else the parse touched, and one `buffer.count` subtraction per access. An invalid lead is rejected here rather than held, which leaves completion with only the second-byte constraints left to check.

next.label: carry it into the next chunk

steps.title: completePendingUTF8
steps.detail: Runs once per chunk, ahead of the dispatch loop, so the bulk loop never tests for it. Continuation bytes are taken off the front of the new chunk until the sequence is as long as its lead says.

next.label: the sequence is whole
next.when: Every byte taken was a continuation and the count reached `sequenceLength(lead)`.

next.label: a non-continuation arrived
next.when: The sequence is truncated: `invalidUTF8`, reported at the lead's offset in the *previous* chunk.

next.label: this chunk ran out first
next.when: A sequence can be cut twice by sufficiently small chunks.

steps.title: hold what arrived
steps.detail: The count advances and the rest waits. Byte-fed input takes this arm three times for a four-byte sequence.

steps.title: invalidUTF8
steps.detail: Reported at the lead, which is a negative offset into this chunk: the parser counts consumed bytes, so an error in a sequence the boundary split still names where the sequence began.

steps.title: the second-byte constraints
steps.detail: The fill loop admitted only continuation bytes and the hold rejected invalid leads, so only overlongs, encoded surrogates and scalars past U+10FFFF remain — the same four tests the contiguous validator applies, without its ASCII prescan, which measured 32% of byte-fed non-ASCII throughput.

steps.title: one stringChunk, from the scratch
steps.detail: The rejoined bytes are emitted from an eight-byte scratch the parser reserves past its buffer's capacity rather than from the input, because half of them are in a chunk that no longer exists. The whole word goes out in one unaligned store and the sink is handed a span of the front of it; the high bytes it will not look at are free to write. A sequence rejoined inside a *skipped* string is validated and dropped.

nodes.title: The windowed walk
why: The dispatcher decides what to do one token at a time. In a document made of short tokens, such as canada.json's coordinate arrays or a mesh, a decision comes every few bytes. Finding every structural byte in a large window first, in one vectorised pass, lets the walk follow a precomputed index instead of making each of those decisions against the bytes.

The step is gated because the trade only pays on structurally dense input. Where strings are long or chunks are small, building the index costs more than it saves, so the parser has to be able to decline it up front and to stop indexing partway through a document when the windows turn sparse.
prose: Chunks of at least `windowThreshold` bytes take this path. The threshold defaults to `.max`, so the windowed walk is opt-in per parser. The block walk's re-probe also lowers it temporarily, to count bulk chunks through the same entry, and in that case the chunk is walked by the ordinary dispatcher.

Measured across the full corpus, the windowed walk loses 4–36% on string-heavy and sub-window payloads: the index costs more to build than the walk saves whenever the document is not structurally dense. It probes density per window and routes sparse windows back to the dispatcher.

next.label: window not dense enough
next.when: Density is probed per window. When the index stops paying for itself the remaining bytes go through the ordinary dispatch loop, which is also what happens for the whole chunk when the gate is off.

nodes.invokes: Indexes a 32 KB window, walks the index rather than the bytes, and measures density as it goes.

steps.title: one scratch allocation
steps.detail: Held on the parser and reused across calls: 32 KB of `UInt32` positions plus two bitmap planes, one for the blocks that need a scan and one for the blocks holding non-ASCII.

steps.title: is the cursor at a token boundary?
steps.detail: A window may start only outside a string with nothing buffered, because the indexer carries no state across windows. Anything else is the dispatcher's.

next.label: the chunk is consumed
next.when: The walk ends where a bulk parse would, with the same events already delivered.

next.label: mid-token
next.when: Inside a string, a buffered number, an escape in flight: one dispatcher step at a time until the cursor is back at a boundary.

next.label: structural, nothing buffered
next.when: The cursor is at a token boundary outside any string, which is the only state the indexer can be started from.

steps.title: one dispatcher step
steps.detail: The same handler the bulk path would have run, so the sink cannot tell which walk produced the events.

steps.title: windowDensity vs 3
steps.detail: Entries per 64 bytes, measured on the last window that was indexed. Census: llm_message 0.7 and gsoc-2018 2.1 against citm 6.0, github 6.4, twitter 7.4 and canada 9.5.

next.label: below 3, probed recently
next.when: String interior with little structure: the index costs more to build than the walk saves, so the span is the dispatcher's.

next.label: dense, or every eighth window
next.when: Every eighth window is indexed regardless, so a document that turns dense again is noticed within one window.

steps.title: hand the span to the dispatcher
steps.detail: Bounded by where the steps stop, not by what they scan — a handler may overrun the span, as a string longer than it would — so the sink sees exactly the chunks a bulk parse produces.

steps.title: stream_parsing_index_window
steps.detail: Stage one, in C: every position the walk must visit, written eight slots at a time. The whole loop is across the boundary because the shuffle it needs takes a target attribute Swift cannot spell.

next.label: walk the index, not the bytes

steps.title: consumeWindow
steps.detail: The dispatcher's structural arms restated over known token extents. It still hands back every token a window cuts and every key with an escape in it — both cold — and the cursor comes back short of the window end when it does.

steps.title: consumeObjectMembers
steps.detail: The object arm of the indexed walk: key, colon and value come out of the index rather than from a scan. The index does not promise a scalar directly after a quote an entry of its own, so the gap between a key's closing quote and its colon is checked before either the key is emitted or the colon consumed — compact JSON takes the adjacent-colon compare and never scans whitespace at all. A complete key and colon can also be the last bytes of an incomplete chunk, so the value is left pending before its first byte is inspected; it belongs to the next parse call. Either check failing hands the cursor back to the dispatcher with the state set, rather than guessing.

steps.title: the chunk is consumed
steps.detail: Same events, same spans, same error reasons and offsets, same rejection points as the unwindowed walk. That contract is why the arms are restated rather than rewritten.

nodes.title: parseDispatching
why: A recursive descent parser keeps its place on the call stack, so being three objects deep inside a string is a chain of return addresses. When a chunk ends mid-document that position has to survive the return from `parse`, and a call stack cannot be suspended and resumed later. This parser keeps its place in data instead: a `state` enum, a `depth`, and a bitmask recording which open containers are objects.

Once the position is data, the parse loop is a switch over it. It reads the state, runs the handler for the token class that state names, and comes back. Every other step on the page chart is one of those handlers or something a handler calls.
prose: The main loop is a switch over the parser's state that calls out to a handler per token class, and then re-enters. The switch is written once, in `dispatchOnce`, which is forced inline into the bulk loop and is also what `parse(byte:)` and the windowed walk's seam run, so the three cannot drift apart. Read on the release binary the dispatcher is a pure dispatcher with no SIMD in it: every token class is a separate function.

Keeping it that way takes explicit attributes, because of register pressure: anything inlined here is paid for by every document, including ones that never execute it. The same state-ladder transformation that made the structural step faster was applied to this loop and measured worse.

next.label: structural states
next.when: `.value`, `.firstValue`, `.afterValue`, `.key`, `.firstKey`, `.afterKey`, `.done` — the states with no token open. They are numbered below the rest so `state.isStructural` is a single unsigned compare.

next.label: .inString / .inKey
next.when: A string body is open. `.inString` streams its bytes and hands a value's first escape to the coalescing tail; `.inKey` goes to `consumeKeyRun`, which buffers so the key can be delivered whole. `.escape` and `.unicode` are separate arms handled one byte at a time.

next.label: .number
next.when: A number is open. This state is entered when the structural run hands back the byte it stopped on — a number is the one token whose first byte belongs to the token itself.

next.label: .skipping …
next.when: The sink declined this subtree. Three states, all placed past `.done` in the enum so that adding them did not cost everyone else the single-compare structural test.

nodes.invokes: `while i < n` calls `dispatchOnce`, a `switch` on `self.state`, forced inline. Exactly one arm runs per iteration; each returns the index it stopped at and the loop tests again, so control comes back here after every run until the chunk is consumed.

steps.title: pending UTF-8 first
steps.detail: Once per chunk, before the loop: a sequence the previous chunk cut is rejoined here so the loop below never has to test for one.

steps.title: dispatchOnce: switch self.state
steps.detail: Thirteen cases over one `UInt8`, lowered as a jump table. Exactly one arm runs per iteration and each returns the new cursor. It is `@inline(__always)` rather than plain `@inlinable`: left to the optimizer the bulk loop called out once per iteration, which is what the loop exists to avoid. The same function is the per-byte loop in `parse(byte:)` and the windowed walk's fall-back seam.

next.label: the seven structural states
next.when: `value`, `firstValue`, `afterValue`, `key`, `firstKey`, `afterKey`, `done` share one arm.

next.label: inString / inKey
next.when: A string value and a key take different arms because one is delivered as a borrowed span and the other is buffered.

next.label: escape / unicode
next.when: One byte per call: an escape selector, or one of the four hex digits.

next.label: number / literal
next.when: A token the run handed back, or one a chunk cut.

next.label: the three skipping states
next.when: Past `done` in the enum on purpose, so `isStructural` stays one unsigned compare.

steps.title: consumeStructuralRun

nodes.title: The structural run
why: Between tokens the parser is in a structural state, expecting a value, a key, a comma, a colon or a close. Those bytes are where the grammar is checked and where container events come from, and in object-heavy JSON they come in runs: `},{"`, `":`, `[[`. If every structural byte went back through the dispatcher, each one would pay for a switch, a call and a return on top of its own work.

The run keeps the loop in one function for as long as the state stays structural, with the nesting held in registers. Everything else on the structural path starts from here: the 64-byte block walk when there is room ahead, the whitespace scan before each byte, and the in-run paths that finish short values without leaving.
prose: Nesting is held in two values: `depth`, and a single `UInt64` where bit *n* is 1 if the container at depth *n* is an object and 0 if it is an array. That is sixty-four levels of nesting in one register. Depth beyond that is rejected rather than spilled, which is why the ceiling exists.

`state`, `depth` and `containers` are copied into locals for the duration of the run and written back on every exit. Left as fields they lived in memory: the release build stored `state` at the end of one byte and loaded it back at the start of the next, and that store-to-load round trip, not the switch, was the loop-carried dependency.

On arm64, and on x86 with the AVX2 classifier, a structural boundary with 64 bytes ahead first enters a block walk. The scalar copy is still the edge path and the authority for anything the classifier declines. The two copies are one `@_transparent` body with a `blocks` literal at each call site, so the scalar copy compiles to the code it was before the walk existed. On x86 the block copy is a call rather than a second inlined body, because inlining both moved `self` out of its register and the scalar loop paid for it.

nodes.title: The structural block walk
why: The scalar structural run still visits every byte between tokens: whitespace behind a compare, then a string scan per key and value. In pretty-printed or object-heavy JSON most of those bytes are not tokens. Classifying 64 bytes at once produces a mask of where each token starts, and the walk jumps from start to start with `trailingZeroBitCount` without looking at the bytes in between.

It sits in front of the scalar run and does not replace it. The scalar copy still handles the last bytes of a chunk, anything the classifier declines, and payloads where classifying does not remove enough work to pay for itself. That last case is why the walk counts strikes and can give up.
prose: One classification replaces the whitespace scan before every token, the string scan before every in-place key or value, and the per-string high-bit reduction. `starts` contains the opening quote or first candidate byte of each token; `quote` pairs string extents; `backslash` decides whether an extent can stay in place. On arm64 the NEON kernel is inlined at the call site; on x86 the AVX2 twin is a call per block.

The grid moves with completed tokens. If a long string or token crosses byte 64, its existing scanner finishes it and the next classification begins at that end rather than at the old fixed boundary. Every classification therefore starts with zero quote and escape carries, and long string interiors are not classified again.

The classifier only pays on shapes where it removes whitespace work. A block with no whitespace outside strings, or at least 48 start candidates, is one strike. Four consecutive strikes store a give-up verdict and the unchanged scalar copy takes over — but not for good: every 64 KB of bulk-sized chunks the verdict is re-armed and the next chunk is walked from its first block, so a stream that changes shape is judged again. A probe that fails again costs four blocks per 64 KB.

nodes.title: The state ladder
why: This is where JSON's grammar is enforced. After `{` only a key or `}` is legal, after a key only `:`, and after a value only a comma or the close that matches the innermost container. Each structural byte is checked against what the current state allows, and it moves `state`, `depth` and the container bitmask to where the next byte will be checked.
It is also where container events reach the sink, and where a byte that begins a value (a quote, a digit, the first letter of a literal) is recognised and routed to the code for that token.
prose: One structural byte, folded into the run loop by force. The states are ordered so that "is this still structural" is a single unsigned compare, which is the only reason their numeric values matter.

Two variants of this same code were measured and rejected: reordering the ladder by what the run actually sees, and peeling the colon out of it. A third — the byte ladder — removes strictly more work and is slower. What the four say together is that this function is limited by its size, not by how many times it iterates.

nodes.title: Values finish in the run
why: In object-heavy JSON most values are short: `"id": 42, "verified": false, "lang": "en"`. When each value left the structural run, it went through the dispatch switch into its own handler and then returned to start a new run for the comma after it. The token is usually complete in the chunk, so that round trip did no work.

This step finishes such a value inside the structural run, emits it, and keeps going. A value the chunk cuts still leaves the run through its ordinary state, because only that state can resume it in the next chunk.
prose: When the ladder reads the first byte of a value, it tries to finish the token in place. A literal needs its four or five bytes in the chunk and is settled with one word compare. A number needs its terminator in the chunk, and is then scanned, parsed and emitted. A string needs its closing quote in the chunk: a clean one is emitted as one `string` call borrowing the input, and one with escapes is decoded without leaving the run. Keys that close in the chunk are read in place the same way.
Twitter gained 11.8% and GSoC lost 2.5%. The obvious fix for that loss was built and measured, and not kept, because it cost Twitter and the pretty-printed payload more than it recovered.

nodes.title: One compare, then out of line
why: JSON allows whitespace between any two tokens, and the grammar only looks at the byte after it. So before each structural byte the parser has to find the next byte that is not whitespace. This runs more often than any other code on the structural path, and on many documents it finds nothing: canada.json has no whitespace, and llm_message's whitespace is all inside strings.

The step splits that work in two. A single compare, cheap enough to sit in the parse loop, settles the case with no whitespace. Only when it fails does the parser call the vector scan, which handles the runs that pretty-printed documents have.
prose: How much whitespace there is to find is a property of the document rather than of JSON: canada has 0%, citm_catalog has 71%, and llm_message has 17%, all of it inside string values where this scan never looks.

Every JSON whitespace byte is ≤ 0x20 and every byte that may legally follow one is > 0x20. So a single compare settles the no-whitespace case without touching a vector, and only what survives is scanned SIMD16 like every other class.

What the *inlined body* costs is the design constraint here, not the scan. This is forced inline into the parse loop, so anything spelled in it is paid in register pressure by every document. Inlining the vector body gains citm 22% and costs twitterescaped 18% and the unicode-escape payload 35%, for code those documents never execute. Moving it out of line recovers both and keeps the gains.

nodes.title: streamStringRun
why: In most JSON documents the majority of bytes are string contents, and the cheapest thing to give a sink is a borrowed span of the input covering a run of them. To hand one over, the parser has to find where the run ends: the first byte it cannot pass through unchanged.

Three bytes end a run. A quote closes the string, a backslash starts an escape whose decoded bytes differ from the input, and a byte below 0x20 is illegal in a JSON string. The scan also has to say whether the run held any non-ASCII byte, because those need UTF-8 validation before a sink may treat the span as text. Keys and string values both go through a scan of this shape.
prose: Sixteen bytes are loaded, compared against a quote, a backslash and the control-byte floor, and the three results are ORed into one mask. A string run ends at the first lane that hits any of the three; if none do, the block is clean and the scan moves on.

SIMD16 was measured against the alternatives at four run lengths and is fastest at all of them. SWAR is worse than scalar below about 12 bytes and never beats SIMD16; SIMD32 loses on arm64 because NEON registers are 128 bits, so a 32-byte vector lowers to two operations plus a recombine.

The scan also answers a second question. It has already loaded every byte, so it carries out whether any had the high bit set, letting a validated ASCII-only string skip a second pass. The flag is exact rather than conservative: bytes after the terminating lane are masked out before the question is asked.

next.when: The mask is non-zero, so the run ends at its lowest set lane. Extracting that lane index is the movemask, and its arm64 spelling is what the assembly tab pins.

next.label: the hit was a backslash
next.when: A backslash ends the run and hands the rest of the string value to `coalescedEscapedStringTail`, which decodes escapes into the parser's buffer and delivers the value per buffer-full.

nodes.invokes: Loads sixteen bytes, ORs three compares into one mask, and answers two questions from that single load: where the run ends, and whether any byte was non-ASCII.

steps.detail: Before any vector setup: a run of length zero is common — an empty string, or the byte right after an escape — and answering it costs one load and three compares against the four splats the body below needs.

next.label: it is one of the three
next.when: The scan returns `from` and the caller reads the terminator itself.

next.label: an ordinary byte
next.when: Not a quote, a backslash or a control byte, so there is a run of at least one byte to scan.

steps.title: while i + 16 <= narrowLimit
steps.detail: The escalation bound, computed once at entry rather than counted per iteration. A counter incremented and tested inside the loop cost citm 2.6% and the 564-byte Qwen payload 5.0% — documents made of short keys that never reach the wide tier at all. Off x86 the bound is `to` and the whole thing folds away.

next.label: a full block remains
next.when: Sixteen bytes are available below the escalation bound.

next.label: fewer than sixteen bytes left
next.when: The chunk end, or on x86 the escalation bound with no full block behind it.

steps.detail: `cmeq` against a quote, `cmeq` against a backslash, `cmlo` against the control-byte floor, then two `orr`. next.when: `any(hit)` is spelled through the shim on arm64: once this body reaches `consumeStructuralRun` the standard library's `any` on a composed mask lost its specialisation and became a call to the generic `SIMD.min`, one `bl` per sixteen string bytes.

steps.detail: The second question, answered from a load already paid for: whether any byte had the high bit set. A validated ASCII-only string skips UTF-8 validation entirely.

steps.title: mask off the lanes past the hit
steps.detail: `lanes .< lane` selects the bytes *before* the terminator, and only those are ORed into the accumulator. That is what makes the non-ASCII flag exact rather than conservative — a `"` followed by high bytes in the same block does not poison the run that ended before them.

steps.title: byte at a time
steps.detail: At most fifteen bytes, each tested against the same three terminators and contributing to the same flag.

steps.title: StreamStringRun
steps.detail: Two fields out of one pass over the bytes.

steps.title: consumeStringRun
steps.detail: The run is emitted as a `stringChunk` unless it ends the string cleanly, in which case one whole `string` record goes out instead. The body is straight-line: every escape leaves it for the coalescing tail, so this is the only scan it makes. The hit-path latency chain here was measured — nine dependent operations and a stack spill, both removed — and the parser did not move: +0.07%.

nodes.title: Finding the lane
why: A vector compare answers whether any of 16 bytes matched, as a mask. The parser needs the position of the first match, because that is where the span handed to the sink ends and where the next token begins. Converting the mask to an index happens once per string, key and number scan, so how it is spelled affects every document.
prose: Once a block hits, the scan needs to know *which* lane. The obvious spelling — loop over sixteen lanes and take the first set one — unrolls into sixteen test/branch pairs plus sixteen constant-materialising exit blocks: over a hundred bytes of branch ladder, walked once per string token and once per key, to produce an integer the machine was already holding.

On arm64 the answer is `vshrn`, which Swift cannot express because its shift is an immediate, so it lives in a C shim. The form that landed fuses the bound check into the lane: an all-ones complement has 64 trailing zeros, which divides to lane 16, one past the block, so the bound check is the terminator test and nothing depends on the branch.

The portable spelling reaches the same answer arithmetically rather than with a select, and the reason is a specific compiler behaviour: written as a ternary, LLVM's x86 cmov-converter turns the intended conditional move back into two branches whenever it judges the condition predictable. On a terminator lane, which is unpredictable by nature, that is exactly wrong.

steps.title: streamMaskBytes
steps.detail: The mask is already sixteen bytes of 0x00 or 0xFF, so the bitcast costs nothing. It exists so both spellings below take the same input and the tests can hold them to one oracle.

next.label: arm64
next.when: The instruction exists, and Swift cannot spell it.

next.label: everywhere else
next.when: No `vshrn`, and no horizontal reduction worth using either.

steps.title: vshrn_n_u16(·, 4)
steps.detail: Sixteen bytes narrowed to eight, four bits per lane, in one instruction. It lives in a C shim because its shift is an immediate, which Swift's SIMD surface has no way to express.

steps.title: trailingZeroBitCount >> 2
steps.detail: The form that landed fuses the bound check into the lane: an all-ones complement has 64 trailing zeros, which divides to lane 16 — one past the block. So `lane` and the branch condition become ready in the same cycle, where testing the mask first leaves `mvn`/`rbit`/`clz` strictly after the branch and a short token pays that chain in full before it can exit.

steps.title: two 64-bit words
steps.detail: The mask reinterpreted as `SIMD2<UInt64>`; each word's trailing zero count is eight lanes' worth of answer.

steps.title: (low >> 3) + ((high >> 3) & lowEmpty)
steps.detail: Arithmetic rather than a conditional move, for a specific compiler reason: written as a ternary, LLVM's x86 cmov-converter turns the intended `cmov` back into two branches whenever it judges the condition predictable. On a terminator lane, which is unpredictable by nature, that is exactly wrong.

nodes.title: Escapes, decoded and coalesced
why: An escape is the one place where the bytes in the JSON and the string's content differ. `\n` is two bytes in the input and one in the value, and `\u00e9` is six bytes in the input and two in UTF-8. The sink is promised decoded content, so from a string's first backslash on the parser can no longer hand over spans of the input. It has to write the decoded bytes somewhere and hand over those.

This step does the decoding and decides how the result is delivered. In real text escapes are short and frequent, so delivering each fragment as its own call would turn one string into dozens of sink calls. Coalescing into the parser's buffer keeps it to one call per buffer-full.
prose: An escape ends the zero-copy string run. From a string value's first backslash on, `coalescedEscapedStringTail` decodes each escape into the parser's own buffer, copies the literal runs between them in behind it, and hands the sink one `stringChunk` per buffer-full rather than one per fragment. `\uXXXX` sequences are decoded to UTF-8 bytes inside the parser — including surrogate pairs, which have to be held across the gap between the two halves and can be cut by a chunk boundary in the middle.

Every sink takes that path. The fragments an escape leaves are tiny — 57% of `llm_message`'s string chunks were a single byte — so an accumulating sink saves many times the copy in calls it no longer makes, while a sink whose calls are nearly free pays for the copy (`FastCountingSink` on LLM message reads ~11% slower). That was judged a better price than a second delivery mode: chunk boundaries were never promised.
Nothing here produces a `Unicode.Scalar` or a `String`. That keeps the Unicode data tables out of the binary, which is what lets the core build under Embedded Swift.

steps.title: the run stopped on a backslash
steps.detail: The string scan ends at the backslash and the selector is the next byte. A string value's backslash sends the rest of the value to the coalescing tail; the per-byte escape states, keys and the windowed walk take the same decoders but emit each escape on its own.

next.label: a string value, selector in the chunk
next.when: `stringRunBody` hands over to `coalescedEscapedStringTail`, out of line by force: spelled inside the run body it cost raw llm 52%.

next.label: the chunk cut it, or a key
next.when: A backslash that is the chunk's last byte leaves for `.escape`; a key's escape is reassembled into the key buffer.

steps.title: coalescedEscapedStringTail
steps.detail: Decodes the escape that sent it here, then loops: scan a run, append it to the buffer, and at the next backslash decode again. The quote flushes the buffer and emits `stringEnd`; so does every other non-throwing exit, so a chunk that cuts the value resumes exactly where fragment-by-fragment delivery would have.

steps.title: fusedEscapeEnd(coalescing: true)
steps.detail: `@inline(__always)`, so the `coalescing` literal folds and no other caller carries the buffered arm. The earlier spelling was a runtime field tested in `emitScratch`, which put a load and a never-taken arm into every escape emitter in the binary, byte-fed dispatcher included: LLM message byte by byte -4.9%. Only escapes with no diagnostic attached fuse; anything else returns nil, the buffer is flushed, and the per-byte states take over.

next.label: `\u` with six bytes left
next.when: Decoded here rather than handed to the per-byte states.

next.label: a simple escape
next.when: One byte out of the escape table, appended to the buffer.

next.label: nil
next.when: A bad selector, a pending high surrogate, or an escape past the chunk end.

steps.title: bufferStringRun
steps.detail: A run of at most sixteen bytes is one unaligned 16-byte load and store rather than a `memmove` call, under two slack checks: sixteen readable bytes before the chunk end, and sixteen writable before the end of the allocation, which is the buffer plus the reserved scratch behind it. A run at least as long as the buffer flushes and goes to the sink in place.

steps.title: consumeEscape
steps.detail: The per-byte spelling, kept for an escape a chunk boundary cuts and for the ones carrying diagnostics. A high surrogate pending here is severed by any escape but a low surrogate, and severing it first is also what keeps the emitted content in order around the error.

next.label: the table has a byte for it
next.when: Written straight into the destination.

next.label: the cell is zero
next.when: `invalidEscape`, reported at the backslash rather than at the selector.

steps.title: streamDecodeSimpleEscape
steps.detail: A byte index into a 128-entry table where zero means "no escape". Exactly eight cells are non-zero, which is the whole of JSON's simple-escape grammar as data rather than as a compare chain.

steps.title: invalidEscape
steps.detail: At `offset - 1`: the backslash, which is where a reader looking at the document would say the escape began.

steps.title: fusedUnicodeEscapeEnd
steps.detail: Outlined, because it is cold relative to the scan it interrupts. The bounds test comes first so the halfword load that follows stays inside the chunk.

next.label: four hex digits
next.when: Six bytes are in the chunk and all four digits parse, so the scalar is known here rather than across four per-byte calls.

next.label: the chunk cut it, or it needs a diagnostic
next.when: A lone low surrogate, or a high surrogate followed by anything but a low one: both are diagnostics, so they go to the per-byte path where the offsets are exact.

steps.title: streamHexQuad
steps.detail: Four bytes at once: the digit range and the letter range tested in parallel, the nibbles selected by mask, then weighted by 0x1000/0x100/0x10/1 and summed. One rejection test covers all four digits.

next.label: a high surrogate
next.when: A pair is twelve bytes and has to be complete and well formed to be fused.

next.label: an ordinary scalar
next.when: Outside both surrogate ranges, so it stands alone.

steps.title: the second escape, in the same call
steps.detail: The `\u` prefix is one halfword compare, then a second `streamHexQuad` and a range test. Only then are the halves combined.

steps.title: consumeUnicodeDigit
steps.detail: One hex digit per call, shifted into `unicodeValue`. A high surrogate is held on the parser across the gap, which is what lets a pair be cut anywhere — including between its two halves.

steps.title: UTF-8 bytes, one store
steps.detail: Nothing here produces a `Unicode.Scalar` or a `String`, which keeps the Unicode data tables out of the binary and is what lets the core build under Embedded Swift. The bytes are assembled little-endian in a register and stored whole in one unaligned eight-byte write. In the coalescing tail that write lands at the end of the parser's buffer (`bufferStringScratch`) — one to four bytes count, and the rest fall past `bufferCount` into the reserved region behind it, never past the allocation. On the per-byte path it lands in that reserved scratch region itself and the sink gets a span of its front. Storing only the bytes that count, with a loop, measured worse on escape-dense corpora: Twitter escaped bulk 1,289 → 1,374 MB/s for the whole-word form. Giving the word its address from a stack local instead cost 10–14%.

nodes.title: UTF-8 validation
why: JSON text has to be UTF-8, and the sink contract passes that guarantee on: keys arrive validated, and every span ends on a character boundary. A destination can then build a `String` or match a key without checking the bytes again. The parser is the only component that sees every byte, so this is where invalid input is rejected: an overlong encoding, a stray continuation byte, a surrogate encoded directly.
Validation runs only where it is needed. The string run already reports whether a span had any byte with the high bit set, and ASCII-only spans never reach this step.
prose: Non-ASCII content is validated in vectors, using Keiser and Lemire's three-nibble-table construction: three table lookups ANDed together, XORed with a continuation requirement derived from leads two and three bytes back. Nonzero lanes are errors.

The one operation Swift cannot express is the byte table lookup itself — on arm64 that is `tbl`, and it lives in a C shim as a leaf returning a vector. Composing the same kernel from Swift's SIMD primitives instead ran 2.6× slower, because Swift's SIMD operators are lane loops that LLVM re-vectorizes, and a compare feeding a fifteen-lane shift came out half vectorized with the last lanes patched one at a time.
What landed here was not a better kernel but a deferred reduction: hoisting the per-block reduction out of the loop measured +5.7%, while a 2× unroll of the same loop measured no change.

steps.title: streamValidateUTF8
steps.detail: Called once per non-ASCII run — a run the string scan already flagged from a load it had already paid for — so an ASCII-only document never reaches this function at all.

next.label: check the run's own end first

steps.title: the last three bytes
steps.detail: The block test sees a lead and never the continuation that is missing past the end of the run, so the last three bytes are checked against what may legally sit there before any block runs.

next.label: arm64
next.when: The table lookup exists.

next.label: no byte-table lookup
next.when: Compares instead.

steps.title: stream_parsing_utf8_block_errors
steps.detail: The whole block kernel in one C leaf returning a vector. Composing the same kernel from Swift's SIMD primitives ran 2.6× slower, because Swift's SIMD operators are lane loops that LLVM re-vectorizes — a compare feeding a fifteen-lane shift came out half vectorized with the last lanes patched one at a time.

steps.title: 3 × tbl, ANDed
steps.detail: Keiser and Lemire's construction: the previous byte's high nibble and low nibble into two tables, this byte's high nibble into a third, and the three results ANDed. An error class survives only where all three tables agree it can.

next.label: the other half of the answer

steps.title: the three nibble tables
steps.detail: Error classes as bit positions: too-long, two-continuations, too-short, overlong 2/3/4, surrogate, too-large. Each table says which classes its nibble *permits*; the AND leaves the ones all three agree on.

steps.title: qsub, orr, eor
steps.detail: Saturating subtraction leaves a high bit exactly where a lead two or three bytes back still owes a continuation. XORing that against the lookup cancels the lanes that have one, so a lane is an error only when the two disagree.

steps.title: one reduction for the whole run
steps.detail: Hoisting the per-block reduction out of the loop measured +5.7%; a 2× unroll of the same loop measured no change. The validator answers only valid-or-not — the parser's scalar walk locates the byte afterwards — so combining the error vectors loses nothing.

next.label: the run is done
next.when: One test, after the loop rather than inside it.

steps.title: streamUTF8BlockIsInvalidPortable

steps.title: any lane non-zero?
steps.detail: Valid or not. Where it is not, the parser walks the run scalar-wise to name the byte.

nodes.title: The greedy scan
why: A number has no closing delimiter. `12` might be the whole token or the start of `12.5e3`, and the parser only knows the token has ended when it reads a byte that cannot belong to a number. So the first job is finding that byte, and when the chunk ends before it, the token's bytes are buffered until the next chunk arrives.

The sink receives each number once, whole, with its digits already accumulated into a magnitude and a decimal exponent (`NumberInfo`). Scanning to the end first and classifying afterwards lets the parser choose a kernel by the token's length and shape, instead of testing for a sign, a dot and an exponent as each byte arrives.
prose: When the terminator is in the chunk, the structural run scans, parses and emits the number without leaving the run. The `.number` state handles the rest: a token the chunk cuts, which is buffered whole, and every number fed one byte at a time. A number is the one token whose first byte belongs to the token itself, so in those cases the run hands that byte back rather than consuming it.

The terminator search uses the same fused movemask as the string scan, and it is the row where that change paid most: floats gained 17.6%. It is also the row that pins the limit. One-to-three-digit tokens lose 7.5% to *any* movemask spelling, because the per-lane ladder's moves issue in parallel with the loop test while a movemask makes the lane strictly serial. Three separate variants confirmed no formulation beats the ladder there.

next.label: ≤ 8 digits, no `.` or `e`
next.when: The entire token fits in one 64-bit word, which is loaded and converted with no loop at all.

next.label: otherwise
next.when: A float, or an integer too long for the word path. Eisel-Lemire produces the `Double` directly; 91% of canada used to build a `String` per number to get here.

nodes.invokes: Scans greedily to the terminator first and classifies afterwards, so the decision reads a length and a digit count instead of walking the bytes a second time.

steps.title: the run hands the byte back
steps.detail: A number is the one token whose first byte belongs to the token itself, so `consumeStructural` returns true, the run steps the cursor back and `.number` re-reads it.

steps.title: streamNumberRunEnd
steps.detail: Greedy: take every byte that could be part of a number, then decide what shape it was. One pass, sixteen bytes at a time.

next.label: find the first byte that is not in the class

steps.title: two nibble tables, vtstq_u8
steps.detail: The high nibble into one table and the low nibble into the other; a lane belongs to the class where the two share a bit. Low nibble 5 carries both the digit and the E/e bits — `'5'` is 0x35, `'E'` is 0x45 — and the high nibble resolves which applies, or neither: `'%'` is 0x25, whose high nibble offers none of them.

steps.title: (~movemask).trailingZeroBitCount >> 2
steps.detail: The bound check *is* the terminator test: a mask of all ones has no terminator, its complement is zero, and `trailingZeroBitCount` of zero is 64 — lane 16, one past the block. Floats gained 17.6% from this form. It is also where the limit sits: one-to-three-digit tokens lose 7.5% to *any* movemask spelling, because the per-lane ladder's moves issue in parallel with the loop test while a movemask makes the lane strictly serial. Three variants confirmed no formulation beats the ladder there.

next.label: a lane terminated the run
next.when: The lane index is below sixteen, which is the same test the fused form makes for free.

next.label: fewer than sixteen bytes left
next.when: The loop bound failed: the token runs into the last fifteen bytes of the chunk.

steps.title: streamNumberRunEndTail
steps.detail: The same five tests per byte, scalar: digit, dot, dash, plus, or E with the case bit forced.

steps.title: the run's extent
steps.detail: One pass has produced the token's bounds; nothing has yet decided whether it is well formed.

next.label: the run reached the chunk end
next.when: The token may continue in the next chunk.

next.label: the run ends inside the chunk
next.when: A byte outside the number class follows, so the token is complete and can be parsed now.

steps.title: copy the bytes into the buffer
steps.detail: A number is the one token the parser copies rather than borrows, because its bytes have to be joined across the boundary before they can be parsed. A document that ends inside a number is settled by `finish()`.

steps.title: decide what shape it was
steps.detail: Sign, integer digits, fraction, exponent — walked once, in order, over bytes already known to be in the class. The result is a `NumberInfo`: the digits with the dot removed, the power of ten they are scaled by, and the flags a destination needs to reject a value its type cannot hold.

nodes.title: Eight bytes, backwards
why: Most numbers in real JSON are small non-negative integers such as ids, counts and indices, and four of the seven corpus payloads are mostly made of them. The general path checks for a sign, a decimal point and an exponent, and accumulates digits one at a time. For a token of one to eight digits a single 64-bit load answers all of that: whether every byte is a digit, and what the value is.
prose: An unsigned integer of one to eight digits is parsed whole, with no loop and no data-dependent branch. The digit test doubles as the shape test, so this *replaces* the structured walk's sign, dot and exponent checks for the tokens it accepts rather than adding to them.

The load is the eight bytes *ending* at the token, not starting at it. Those bytes are behind the cursor — already-consumed input in the same buffer — so a single `end >= 8` test makes the read safe, where reading forward would need a bound the parser does not carry. Right alignment also removes the scaling step: the masked-off bytes below the token become leading zeros, so the digit tree's answer is already the value.

The mask must come before the bias. Subtracting `0x30` from the whole word borrows out of any byte below `'0'` — newline, comma and quote all qualify — and into the token's leading digit, so `582` preceded by a newline reads as `482`. A differential test over random junk prefixes found this; reasoning about the kernel did not, which is why the tests pad with hostile bytes rather than spaces.

steps.title: length ≤ 8, and end ≥ 8
steps.detail: The second test is what makes the backwards load safe: the eight bytes *ending* at the token are already-consumed input in the same buffer, where reading forward would need a bound the parser does not carry. Spelling the first as an unsigned range test in the caller was measured and reverted — it cost one `lea` on the entry guard that every number pays, including the fractional ones that never reach here.

next.label: both hold
next.when: One to eight bytes long, and at least eight bytes of the buffer sit behind the token's end.

next.label: anything else
next.when: A sign, a dot, an exponent, or more than eight digits: the structured walk.

steps.title: load 8 bytes ending at `end`
steps.detail: One unaligned `UInt64`. The token is right-aligned inside it and whatever preceded it in the document fills the rest.

steps.title: keep = ~0 << shift
steps.detail: A masking shift, not the smart one. A token is one to eight bytes so `shift` is 0…56 and the over-shift case cannot arise — but the compiler cannot see that range from here and emitted the defence: `xor`, `cmp rax,0x40` and a `cmovb` in front of the `and` that every other operation waits on. Removing it also let the shift amount fall to eight bits, so five instructions left the critical path.

steps.title: (word & keep) − (0x3030… & keep)
steps.detail: The mask must come before the bias. Subtracting `0x30` from the whole word borrows out of any byte below `'0'` — newline, comma and quote all qualify — and into the token's leading digit, so `582` preceded by a newline reads as `482`. A differential test over random junk prefixes found this; reasoning about the kernel did not, which is why the tests pad with hostile bytes rather than with spaces.

steps.title: ((biased + 0x7676…) | biased) & 0x8080…
steps.detail: One test for all eight bytes: any byte outside `0…9` leaves a high bit set. The digit test doubles as the shape test, so this *replaces* the sign, leading-zero, dot and exponent checks rather than adding to them.

next.label: all eight were digits
next.when: Every masked byte was in `0…9`, which also settles that the token has no sign, dot or exponent.

next.label: any byte was not
next.when: Whatever it was — a sign, a dot, an `e` — the structured walk names it.

steps.title: three multiplies
steps.detail: Pairs, then quads, then the whole word: `2561`, `6553601`, `42949672960001`. Right alignment also removes the scaling step, because the masked-off bytes below the token became leading zeros — so the tree's answer is already the value, with no loop and no data-dependent branch anywhere in the kernel.

steps.title: streamAccumulateDigits
steps.detail: Eight digits at a time while they last, then one at a time. Used for the integer part and again for the fraction, accumulating into the same magnitude — which is what makes `exponent` a subtraction rather than a second pass.

steps.title: streamParseEightDigits
steps.detail: The same pair/quad/word tree as above, over a `SIMD8<UInt8>` biased by subtracting `'0'` from every lane at once.

nodes.title: Floats without a String
why: The parser does not know what type a number is going to. It emits the digits as a 64-bit magnitude and a power-of-ten exponent, and the destination converts them. When the destination is a `Double` or a `Float`, the conversion has to produce the correctly rounded binary value, the same one `Double("…")` would produce. In float-heavy payloads like canada.json it runs once per coordinate.

The conversion is tiered. When the magnitude and the power of ten are both exactly representable, one multiply or divide gives the exact answer. Past that, Eisel–Lemire computes the result with 128-bit arithmetic against a table of powers of ten. Only an input it cannot decide, or one with more than nineteen digits, falls back to parsing a `String`.
prose: A census of canada.json found 91% of its numbers were building a Swift `String` per `Double` to parse them. Replacing that with Eisel-Lemire measured 3.15× on the path. The same census found the corpus contains zero exponents, which bounds what further work here can be worth.

The power-of-ten table lives in C, not Swift. A Swift array global is not a constant expression, so every read routes through a lazy-initialisation accessor — a call, on a path that is otherwise branch-free. Moving the table into a C translation unit is what removed it.

The conversion is generic over the destination, and `Float` is not narrowed from `Double`: decimal to `Double` to `Float` rounds twice and is not correctly rounded in general. The kernel is parameterised on the binary format the way fast_float's is, so every constant folds to an immediate once the type is known and the `Double` specialisation is the hand-written kernel instruction for instruction.

steps.title: emitNumber already holds the inputs
steps.detail: `NumberInfo` carries the digits with the dot removed and the power of ten they are scaled by, which is exactly the form the kernel wants — so nothing re-walks the token. The float conversion reads it for any `BinaryFloatingPoint` destination.

next.label: magnitude and exponent exact in T
next.when: One multiply or divide by a power of ten the destination represents exactly: 10^22 for `Double`, 10^10 for `Float`, the last power whose factor of five fits the significand. Both bounds are constants per type rather than `init(exactly:)` calls, which were an out-of-line range check and a NaN test on a table entry.

next.label: anything else
next.when: 91.2% of canada.json's numbers, each of which was building a Swift `String` and calling the standard library's parser. Replacing that measured 3.15× on the path.

steps.title: scale by a representable power of ten
steps.detail: Kept ahead of the kernel because it is shorter, and because it is the path every small integer and short decimal takes.

steps.title: stream_parsing_pow10_double
steps.detail: The exact-path scales, in C for the same reason as the 128-bit table below.

nodes.title: StreamParseSink
why: The parser's job ends at tokens; what they become is the destination's business. A typed `@StreamParseable` struct, a counter in a benchmark and a hand-written sink that wants one field all consume the same token stream. The protocol is the boundary between them, so the parser can be specialised for any destination without knowing what it builds.

Streaming shapes it. A token's bytes live in the chunk being parsed and are invalid once `parse` returns, so the sink borrows them rather than receiving a copy, and `commit()` tells it when that memory is about to go away.
prose: The parser's whole output surface: one method per token class, each carrying a borrowed `Span<UInt8>` that is invalid the moment the call returns. It is format-agnostic rather than JSON-specific, so another parser could drive the same sinks.

No method throws. A check after every call sits on the hottest path — measured at 2–5% — so a sink records its failure and the parser polls it at token boundaries instead, reporting the failure at the token that provoked it. Sinks record a bool from their apply members rather than throwing, which is what distinguishes a key the destination doesn't have (ignored) from a field that cannot hold this kind of value (a type mismatch).

There is exactly one form per token. A key is always whole; a string always arrives as begin/chunks/end, or as one call when it is complete and escape-free in the chunk. Where the chunks fall carries no meaning — after a value's first escape the parser coalesces its content and delivers one chunk per buffer-full. The collapsed forms both protocols once declared are gone — one because no parser could keep the promise, the other because in two rounds of parser work nothing ever called it.

nodes.title: Skipping a subtree
why: A typed destination often wants only part of a document. An API response carries nested objects a struct may not declare. Without a way to say so, the parser would resolve every key inside them and emit every string, and the sink would discard each one.

A disposition lets the sink answer once, at the opening bracket. `PartialSink` answers `.skip` for a container under a key its schema does not have, and the parser switches to a walk whose only job is finding the matching close.
prose: Both container opens return a disposition. A sink with no use for a subtree's interior answers `.skip`, and the parser scans past it at structural speed: no keys resolved, no strings emitted, no values built.

The answer is advisory on purpose. A `.skip` may still be followed by the interior (the batching adapter's replay delivers it), but the matching close *always* arrives, so a sink is never left with an unbalanced frame. A skipped interior is validated structurally: brackets match by kind, strings terminate, control bytes and invalid UTF-8 are rejected, and the depth cap holds. Number grammar, escape selectors and comma and colon placement are not checked.

nodes.title: Keys, in place
why: Every object member starts with a key, and the key is how a typed destination finds out which stored property the following value belongs to. That lookup runs once per member of every object in the document, so on object-heavy payloads it is one of the most frequent operations in the typed layer.
This is why the parser always delivers a key whole. A destination matching against a set of names needs the complete, unescaped bytes, not a first fragment it would have to reassemble.
prose: A key is always delivered whole — unescaped, validated UTF-8 — and matching it against a schema's members does not use a `Dictionary`. Keys are compared as precomputed 64-bit words, which for the overwhelming majority of real keys means one or two compares.

The read happens in place, out of the parser's buffer, using padding the buffer already had and nobody was reading. Where that read lives turned out to be the entire result: the same code in a different function could not hold the branch.

A block key match was built and measured against this, and lost: a predicted scan over eight or fewer entries beats a latency chain. The object-heavy bottleneck is not the key match — it is what happens after the key resolves.

nodes.title: Schemas, borrowed
why: Tokens name members by string, while a Swift value is stored properties at byte offsets. Something has to connect the two for each type: which key goes to which property, what kind of value that property holds, and how to enter a nested object or an array element. It has to be available at runtime to a sink that is generic over the root type. `@StreamParseable` generates that description once per type, and the schema is that description.
The sink reads a schema at every container open and every key, so how it is held matters as much as what it contains.
prose: A schema describes how a type's members map onto tokens. It is a reference rather than a value, and frames borrow it `unowned(unsafe)` — a retain and release per container open was showing up in the profile.

Two rewrites were measured and rejected: replacing the closures with a witness metatype, and a family of alternative unowned spellings. What did work was narrower — a borrowed frame type, plus a tripwire to catch the lifetime assumption if it stops holding.
Two codegen traps are recorded here: taking a strong parameter from an `unowned(unsafe)` source reintroduces the retain, and `if let` on an `unowned(unsafe)` optional does the same.

An element's initial value is a pointer, not a closure: one template per schema, allocated once and leaked, copied straight into the element's slot. That replaced a pair of initial-value closures chosen per element type, which is itself a landed experiment the closures were the result of.

nodes.title: PartialSink
why: The token stream is flat. `key`, `beginObject`, `number` and `endObject` carry no record of where in the document they sit. To build a nested Swift value, the destination has to keep that record itself, tracking which container it is in and which member the next value belongs to. It also has to write each token into the value as it arrives, so the partial value is readable after every chunk.

`PartialSink` keeps that record as a stack of frames, one per open container, each holding a pointer into the value being built and the schema that describes it. It is the `StreamParseSink` the typed layer ships. A hand-written sink implements the protocol directly and never goes through it.
prose: The typed layer's sink: it keeps a spine of frames, each pointing into the partially built value, and turns tokens into stores. A container entry is now the frame itself — bits rather than references — and scalars whose kind is known at schema-build time are stored directly instead of going through a general applier.

Six codegen traps are recorded against this file. Among them: a struct nested inside the generic sink lowers to a value-witness destroy; `init(rawValue:)` on a decoded enum is not free; and a `count <= 8` branch causes the scan behind it to unroll.

nodes.invokes: Keeps a spine of frames, each pointing into the partially built value, and turns tokens into stores. A container entry is the frame itself — bits rather than references.

steps.title: a container opens: push a frame
steps.detail: A `BorrowedFrame` is storage, an `unowned(unsafe)` schema, the pending field and a packed route word — 24 bytes. It is trivial, so pushing and popping is a store and a decrement rather than an ARC pair, and deinitializing the stack is a no-op. The storage pointer is the load-bearing part: only the innermost open container is ever mutated, so an element pointer stays valid for that element's lifetime — appending to an outer array cannot happen while an inner one is open — and a copy of the value taken *between* parse calls cannot invalidate one either, because every container holds its open element inline at a fixed offset in storage the stream owns, so the copy diverges and the address the frame holds still names the parser's own element.
