nodes.title: StreamString
why: A string member of a partial value grows while the document streams: an LLM's response text arrives a few bytes per chunk. Keeping that member as a Swift `String` would mean decoding the new bytes into it on every chunk, with growth that can reallocate and copy everything written so far. `StreamString` stores the bytes the parser already validated, and produces a `String` only when something reads one.
prose: Bytes accumulate; producing a `String` is a read, not a side effect. Storage grows in blocks whose size doubles, so a long streamed string does not pay a reallocation per chunk.

In the allocation census the block ramp was the smaller half of the cost. The larger sources were the bookkeeping array tracking the blocks and a tail reserve on the fragment-fed path. Fixing those measured +11.2% on the LLM message and +5.5% on GSoC.

The accumulated bytes are also readable as the words a generated matcher compares, which is what lets `@StreamParseable` on a raw-`String` enum emit the same shape of matcher for a case name that it emits for an object key.

steps.detail: `String.streamAppend` is `self += String(decoding:)` — a whole intermediate `String` built and destroyed per chunk, re-validating UTF-8 the parser already validated, ~61 ns per content byte under byte-fed input.

steps.detail: A fixed-capacity string whose storage the parser appends into directly, for a member that declares its own ceiling.

steps.title: promoteSizedInlineStorage
steps.detail: The first overflow sizes the schedule's start: a value that arrives as one big span starts on a block matched to half its size instead of walking the whole doubling ramp, while a fragment-fed value keeps the 512-byte start and lets the ramp absorb growth. Outlined, because promotion happens once per value and its body inlined into every `stringChunk` call site is exactly the growth that flips the parse loop's inlining.

steps.title: appendBlocked
steps.detail: Fill the tail, seal it, start the next. The physical layout can differ between hinted, unhinted and differently-fed values, so every physical boundary is a multiple of 512 and reads, equality, ordering and hashing use canonical 512-byte logical windows.

steps.title: reserve the block, not the fragment
steps.detail: An empty tail reserving only what the fragment needs is right for the *first* block and wrong for every one after it: a seal empties the tail, so a fragment-fed value re-entered that arm at every block and grew in 512-byte steps, paying a reallocation per block. Escape-split values are exactly the ones that hit it. LLM message +11.2%, GSoC +5.5%.

next.label: the tail reached its capacity
next.when: The block is full, and a full block is never written again.

next.label: the fragment fit
next.when: Nothing sealed; the tail keeps growing.

steps.title: blocks.append(tail); capacity <<= 1
steps.detail: Doubling, capped at 8 KiB. `blocks` reserves four up front, because it grew by doubling from its first append and a three-block value paid two array reallocations for a spine that was the *other* larger half of the census.

steps.title: one clz, not a search
steps.detail: The schedule is a pure function of the first block's shift and the block index, so locating a byte stays closed form rather than a search over prefix sums.

steps.title: producing a String is a read
steps.detail: Bytes accumulate; decoding happens once, when someone asks. Accumulating raw bytes and decoding at read was the floor the append benchmarks found, ~7× under the append path at small chunks.

steps.title: paddedWord, then isPrefix
steps.kicker: the read side of the key encoding
steps.detail: The same little-endian, zero-padded eight-byte encoding a key span produces, read back out of the accumulated bytes — so a generated matcher compares an accumulated value against a compile-time literal with the identical codegen it already uses for object keys: a `switch` on the leading word, a count check, then any remaining words. The count check is not optional, because an accumulated value may hold a decoded NUL and the padding is otherwise indistinguishable from one. Unlike a key span, whose bytes are a borrow into the document with more document behind them, an accumulated value's last block ends where the value does, so the window is clamped rather than overread. `isPrefix(of:)` is the direction a *streaming* match needs and the mirror of `hasPrefix`: whether what has arrived so far is still consistent with a case name, not whether the name has already arrived. A matcher walks its cases shortest-first asking it, and declines outright on zero bytes — an empty accumulation is a prefix of every case, so answering would be a definite answer on no evidence that then changes as the real bytes land.

nodes.title: Arrays and dictionaries
why: `PartialSink`'s frames point directly into the value being built. For an array that is sound: its buffer can only move on an append, and no append happens while an element is still open. For a `Dictionary` it is not, because an insert can relocate every value. `StreamDictionary` keeps values append-only so the array's rule holds for it as well, and it keeps insertion order.

Both collections also serve the partial value's readers. A sealed block is shared by retaining and never written again, so a snapshot taken mid-stream does not copy the elements that are already complete. Only the block still being filled can be written, and only that one is copied, and only when the append that needs it finds it shared.
prose: Streaming collections with their own storage. Closed elements live in uniform power-of-two blocks a copy shares by retaining, and the one element the parser is still writing lives inline, outside them.

The dictionary's index is a single table with one entry buffer; `Dictionary` was measured against it and lost outright. Both structural guesses made when designing that table turned out to be wrong, and one of them has since been reversed again — the values are blocked now.

Moving the open element into the blocks was built, measured and reverted. What stayed is the block type it needed. The rule built around it did not: a shared block was written past rather than copied, until a review showed that two copies of one array compute the same next slot. The commit path takes an ordinary uniqueness check now, and the discarding collection rows show what that costs.

nodes.invokes: Streaming storage with its own index: a single table with one entry buffer, measured against `Dictionary` and faster.

steps.title: the open element lives outside the storage
steps.detail: `pending` is held inline, so the parser's frame points at a slot no other value can see and its address survives every append — and a plain copy of the value diverges it for free, with no allocation and no bookkeeping, which is the whole reason a snapshot is a struct copy. The schema opens the next element with `_openElement(copying:)`: the closed element moves into its slot and the schema's template is copied into the space it vacated, two whole-element copies with the optional's tag left alone. A whole number token skips the round trip through `_appendClosed`. Opening the element in the storage instead was built and measured: it bought a third on the largest partials and cost 59–72% on every row that *keeps* a snapshot, because the divergence then has to be bought back with a heap block per retained snapshot.

next.label: an array element closed
next.when: The frame's destination is a `StreamArray`, so the pending element is committed into the filling block.

next.label: a dictionary value closed
next.when: The frame's destination is a `StreamDictionary`, whose slot was opened when the key arrived rather than now.

steps.title: commit into the filling block
steps.detail: Closed elements live in uniform power-of-two blocks. A sealed one is never written again, so sharing it is free and a snapshot keeps the elements it already holds for the price of a retain. The filling block is the one that can still be written, and `nextSlot` makes it unique before it returns an address — the check happening before the tail is bound to a local reference, since binding first makes the check answer about the reference it just created. That check used to be absent: each array held its *own* count of the elements in the filling block, the parser appended above the prefix every sharer had captured, and the copy was argued away. Two copies of one array compute the same next slot, so the argument was wrong — `[1]` copied, then `2` appended to one and `3` to the other, reads back `[1, 3]` — and no serial fix covers two threads doing it. The check costs 9–13% on the collection rows that keep nothing at all, where no tail is ever actually copied, and one detached block per retained snapshot on the rows that keep everything. The power is chosen per element type: 32 by default, but a trivial element of at most sixteen bytes aims at 2 KB instead (256 `Double`s), because at 32 `prepareSlot` was 4% of typed Mesh and such a block has no destroy loop to outweigh the allocations saved. A power of two means the sealed count is `blocks.count << shift` and needs no stored field.

next.label: and that is already a snapshot

steps.title: StreamBlock
steps.detail: A `ManagedBuffer` with the elements tail-allocated, not a `ContiguousArray`. An array never exposes its spare capacity, so committing meant handing the element to `append` and letting the array copy it in — and a shared array copies *all* of its elements before the first of those writes. Owning the capacity outright is what lets the parser write the element into the slot it will live in, and what bounds the copy a shared tail now takes to one block. One object rather than two: the two-allocation form doubled the malloc count of every number-heavy corpus (Canada 2,659 → 5,109) and cost them 10–28%. The header is read through its pointer rather than as a stored class property, which from outside its module is a dynamic `swift_beginAccess` even in release, and it is deliberately not generic over the element, because a generic header makes the elements' offset a metadata question wherever the block is reached unspecialised — 7–8% on GitHub and GSoC. A block's `deinit` is emitted once, generically, so it destroys its elements with one counted `deinitialize(count:)` — a `move()` loop there lowered to an alloca, a take and a destroy per element, 1.19 MB of memmove per Twitter full parse.

steps.title: one entry buffer, one slot table
steps.detail: Byte-keyed slots rather than a `[String: Int]`: 12 to 17 ns per hit against 34 to 42, flat in key count, and no allocation on a lookup where a `Dictionary` materialises a `String` for one. The table is empty below the index threshold rather than `nil`, because every unwrap of an optional buffer was a retain that made it non-unique for the next write; a new key opens with one copy of the schema's `.some` template instead of about five whole-value passes. `pendingSlot` is an existing slot when the key repeats, which is what keeps `{"a":1,"b":2,"a":3}` in its original order.

and that is already a snapshot

steps.title: blocking cost 2×; one buffer beat two
steps.detail: Both structural guesses made when designing that table were wrong. Blocking the storage the way the array does cost 2× on the discarding path, because a dictionary reads its storage back on every lookup where an array never reads at all. And a retained state's cost tracks the *number* of buffers it shares, not their size, so the key and its hash travel together and the table is one array rather than a heads-and-next pair.

steps.title: the values are blocked too
steps.detail: `storedValues` is a `StreamArray`, for the reason the elements are: a snapshot shares the sealed blocks instead of copying them. That reverses one of the two guesses above — a flat `[Value]` makes a snapshot-per-byte parse copy the whole value array per byte, measured at 58% off the dictionary snapshot rows, and the 2× finding had no snapshot row in front of it. The dictionary still keeps its *own* open value rather than borrowing the array's, because a repeated key's open value is an element the array already holds, and unlike an append a write into one of those is a write a kept state can see. That write happens inside the drain, with the block it lands in made unique first, so no state can be taken between the check and the write.

steps.title: a plain value copy
steps.detail: Everything left of the parse cursor is immutable, so copying the value retains the blocks rather than copying them — which is why nothing here has a `streamSnapshot()`. The one thing the copy has to diverge is the element the parser is still inside, and holding that inline diverges it for free. `Sendable` is asserted rather than checked here, because the blocks are objects: what makes sharing one safe is that every write into a block makes it unique first, its initialised count included, which is a rule the type system cannot see.

nodes.title: Views and snapshots
why: The point of a streaming parser is reading the value before the document ends, and a reader usually wants one field: the text so far, or the latest element. Copying the whole partial value for each read would cost in proportion to everything parsed so far, on every read. A view lends the reader the value in place for the duration of a closure instead.
Snapshots remain for readers that need a value outliving the parser's next write, such as an async sequence yielding each partial.
prose: Reading a partially parsed value costs what is read. Every parseable type has a `~Copyable`, `~Escapable` view — in practice a typed pointer into the value — that cannot outlive the call that lent it, so reading a field does not copy the document.

Snapshots are the alternative: the async sequence conveniences take a full one per element, because an escaping value has to own its storage. The freeze-the-completed-prefix work is what reduced their cost.
